88	- **Appendix I's small items.** `TotalComparison` extends `StandardMinMax[\TotalComparison\]` in the api and the component, its five restated members kept, so that it gets back `MIN` and `MAX` (row 461 closed; built; taken on the coordinator's recommendation, and he wants it explained in more detail when he has the energy, "I need to pay that down", so it is on the list for his review).
89	
90	### How we work
91	
92	- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test. The test needs no commit of its own: the order is test written, seen failing through the harness, the fix, the test seen passing, and the test and the fix may land in one commit ("I don't recall asking for test and fix to be separated into different commits ... I would worry about increasing the ceremony burden").
93	- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.
94	- **Nothing is built or run twice on the same code.** "We don't want to re be rebuilding stuff that doesn't need to be rebuilt." The design, agreed with him and built into the batch script: the old code, the batch's base, is built once per batch, by the coordinator, before the launch, in a worktree nobody compiles or runs in (the script's `args.baseBuild`); "We just mechanically take the latest build and share it between each rung from the same baseline": every rung worktree is seeded from that one build in seconds (`coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean (his "Duh!" to "seeding a worktree by copying a built tree rather than rebuilding it"); the worker builds only what its own edit changed; the skeptic builds nothing, "very smart skeptics that just like reuse everything that was built during the rank phase as much as possible and just do their independent checks": it reads test-first from the worker's transcript, runs its own small programs on the new code with the rung's build and on the old code against the batch's one base build, through the rung's private seeded copy of it so that no two agents compile into one cache; the second skeptic checks only the repair against its own refusal; no stage re-runs a build, a suite or a measurement on a code state another stage has already run, and no agent reads again a log of output that has not changed: "I want to eliminate all waste of this type. Where we are re-executing stuff for no reason." How a worktree is seeded and what a worker clears after an edit or a failed build is engineering, measured before it is built into the batch script (`coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`; the blinded engineers' variants in `coordinator/process-engineering/cache-sharing.md`).
95	- **The coordinator watches what it launches.** Only a long or large run the coordinator launches outside a batch, a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more, is watched against the estimate it was launched with, so that none runs away as probe P1 did (`coordinator/process-engineering/p1-cost.md`); when it passes its estimate the coordinator reacts, by an instruction to the worker or a stop, and its brief carries what keeps it efficient, a wait polled under the prompt cache's life among it. Ordinary workers carry no such procedure, and no ask is added before a probe: "I don't want you to become paranoid about running probes"; "I don't want the cargo cult of ... monitoring here. Only longer runs. ... I don't want you to burden with ... procedure on each call to workers." P1's waste was one the worker knew how to avoid: "an instruction to that worker would have corrected it."
96	- **A deeper pass, not a halt.** When something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch, no bisection of commits: "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle, no stop: "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one." What reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.

97	- **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
98	- **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
99	- **The mission briefing.** "this whole exercise is about in-context learning. You were not pre-trained on Fortress. And the language was not finished." The planner, who has the whole map, gives each rung a mission briefing from the map that its agents read in their first turn; the share of agents that use it is reported with each landing (it was about 80% once and fell to 25-35%: "We need to get back to that level"). The briefing is in neutral words, "the decisions on record" ("I am trying to stay humble and I don't want to see my name in there multiple times. Make this neutral."); the worker answers no required questions about its search ("I disagree with the procedural enforcement here ... it's giving the agent side quests that it's graded on instead of something that it should just take into consideration during the implementation"; the briefing says "this is not a Java, this is not a Scala, you are in unfamiliar territory", and then the worker "should focus on its tasks"); the skeptic checks the result against the library's way, the ledger and sibling sites, and the decisions on record.
100	- **No re-measuring what the record holds.** "you are wasting resources on remeasuring." A brief hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite and names the one new thing to measure; a clean worker is clean of our options, not of our measurements (protocol principle 5). A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before and does not re-run the stage on an unchanged base; the gate commits its per-site list so that the before is complete. The nine steps are a way to brief him on unfamiliar ground, a type-theoretical question answered from the theory, the rule and a few declarations; and one global rule is sought from type theory and the peers' implementations rather than a rule slapped on a rule ("I cannot be trusted to derive a rule that wouldn't break the whole system and be a hodgepodge of edge cases").
101	- **Reversible stops do not hold a batch.** A stop a batch record reserves for him (a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, an interpreter output a rung cannot account for): "These don't need me now. They are reversible things I can review later. Don't block start of next batches on these." It lands, the push and the next batch go ahead, and it is listed for his review (the protocol's first hard rule). An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop but a ledger row ("we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held"); a rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
102	- **Which decisions taken inside the work reach Pavol, and how.** A decision an agent takes is consequential when it reverses a decision on record, bends it or reads it anew; changes a line of the model program; touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation; chooses among ways the record does not settle; or cannot be undone. Everything else an agent decided is listed for later review, a rung's small items in the ledger, and holds nothing up. A consequential decision reaches Pavol one of three ways: asked before the work, a fork known in advance probed and put in the ask form before the batch is briefed; landed, then reviewed, one that can be undone landing, named in one line at the landing, listed in PLAN under the batch's list with the default that landed and put to Pavol later, one per message; or a stop that holds the work, one that cannot be undone or would act against Pavol's word, put at once. The `coordinator` skill states it (`decisions.md`, "Decisions and how they reach the curator").
103	- **A blocking second review does not hold a green batch.** "we have enough rigor or robustness and backup in our processes after that, so that small failure in a rule should not be blocking ... landing large ships like this." After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for his review, and the post-batch review follows. A red gate after its repair still stops a batch. Built into `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual. The merged-diff review itself stays inside the batch, once, beside the gate, as the check of the merged tree's records, the stops and the routing before the push; removing it and moving its checks to the review after the batch is not taken (Fable's review of the batch practice against the Opus review's; he sided with Fable).
104	- **A tests-only repair does not rerun the gate.** "we are being overly pedantic for no good reason with like how the gates are set up ... we have to be weighing costs and benefits and we are not skipping the test, we are adding the test, we are moving stuff to following batches, we are running reviews after the fact, so we will catch stuff that the rerunning of a gate is not." A repair after the gate that changes no source, library, checker, interpreter or specification file runs its new tests in the harness on the merged tree; the first gate's tables stand; the landing records the new tests beside them; a repair that changes code reruns the gate. The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to every rule of the batch workflow. Built.
105	- **What a batch commits.** "the commit discipline in a branch should not be different from what you will be committing to the main. Like don't keep temporary shit around. We are backing up the transcripts anyway from all the workers. So if we need to dig up something, how the worker arrived at some point, we have the full transcripts." A worker commits, on its own branch as on `main`, only what `main` is to hold: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script or tool that is reusable ("If that script that batch contributes a script that is reusable, it goes in there", such as the documented way of running the checker as a shadow); no captured outputs, logs, raw outputs, script copies or other scratch are committed anywhere; new issues go to the ledger, reports into the batch's report; the process, and whether a worker wrote its test first and saw it fail, is read from the workers' transcripts, which the backup keeps. Deleting the `wip/` branches after a gate is his own chore in the GitHub web page, and he is not reminded of it. Built into the script, its manual and the protocol.
106	- **Workers commit their own files as they go.** "Workers should be committing themselves as they go, focused their files only. Protects against container failures and stops from harness bothering you about uncommitted files." They push to their own `wip/` branches as they work; the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the coordinator pushes `main` every few minutes ("I hope we are committing as we go because I worry that the container will get reset"). A protocol hard rule.
107	- **Which tier runs what.** "You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." The highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier, because that is the work it is for. Workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof"; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls". Sonnet is the tier for archaeology. Two workers launched on the wrong tier once cost him 1.7 million tokens "down the drain". The coordinating session runs on Opus, so that Fable's own weekly pool is kept "for more important work"; it moves to Fable at his word when the pool on all models is spent, and how the Opus trial is judged is in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`.
108	- **The judge's rulings.** A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable ("Second ruling is for Fable."), named in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` (`judgeTier`), so Fable is spent only when a second ruling happens. The review's judge rules while the gate runs on, and the gate writes its outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage. A second repair round is not taken; option (b), approvals with required corrections when the fix is already written, has not been put to him (parked, `PLAN.md`).
109	- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
110	- **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
111	- **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s: batch 8 next. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
112	- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
113	- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
114	- **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
115	- **Check-ins and stops.** A series of check-ins is spaced 45 minutes apart, since hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price; the one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
116	- **Where the work lives.** The work runs in the container on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it; transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded`, "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts?", and the lineages are joined at analysis time; the container recovery procedure is a lesson about the remote container (`coordinator/remote-container.md`), not a ledger row. Everything of ours is under `explorations/` ("to remove confusion for any workers"); the inventory note's own move list waits on his reading (parked, `PLAN.md`). Later, a cleaner pass: `main` holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, the whole process record lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of `main` with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress; GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches. A post-mortem index points into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that regenerates any verbatim view; the transcript is not restated.
117	- **The record is public and names models on purpose.** The protocol's rule against model identifiers is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here.
118	- **The record's form: an optimized build and a debug build.** FACTS and POSITIONS are the optimized build, "what is true about the repository snapshot at this moment in time", written timelessly: no dates, no provenance, no account of what changed when or what corrected what; the history files are the debug build, with the full provenance, his quotes at their dates and every earlier text. "I don't want you to be searching with a flashlight in a dark room. I want to give you a map of the territory." A worker or a coordinator appending to FACTS or POSITIONS needs no timestamps; where one is written, or an entry corrects an earlier one, the next consolidation moves that provenance into the history and rewrites the fact or the position without it, at full informational fidelity. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since workers read it and pay the cost. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, pointing to the report or record that holds the detail, and the rung entries already in the file are shortened so, each earlier text verbatim in the history, before batch 8 launches: his choice of option 2 when the growth history showed the batches' rung entries, about 14 KB a landed batch, as most of FACTS' growth. The files read at every boot hold a clean current state and do not need edits as the work moves; the narrative of how a landed rung established a fact is history.
119	- **The statement for the public record on the usage limit.** "let the public record state that I'm now doing unpaid testing job of Anthropic's cloud infrastructure in my open source repository that is normally doing open source research of agentic coding capabilities." The account's weekly limit on all models stopped a running batch after its rung workers; later turns and subagents were served while the limit still read reached; he did not activate the promotional credit the panel offered, and his reading since is that visiting its page activated it unknowingly and that the work served was the $250 promotional credit for the cloud product, support having told him the offer had expired, "which was not true" (`coordinator/usage-metering-2026-09-30.md`, "After the report"); the container was booted afresh at each wake once nothing kept the session busy; at his word the batch was resumed to see whether it survives such interruptions and finishes.
120	
121	## How he wants to be spoken to
122	
123	- **The register.** "Drop the smart Alec essayist register before I blow a fuse": plain sentences, no framing flourishes, no closing lines that sum up in a phrase; advice as instructions, not as observations; replies very brief, plain English, no internal jargon. A wall of text is one he cannot absorb; the failure mode "is focused on over-compressing into a clever turn of phrase, but utterly fails in communicating clearly." Label which part answers which question when several are asked; do not restate what is in this file or in FACTS.md; when a concept is new to him, define it (he asked for reshape, ravel, planes, gather, outer product, Ring, Field, nat parameters, matrix multiplication).
124	- **Asks and decisions.** Decisions are presented one at a time as: what we do, what it changes, with a default he can accept without reading the argument; the argument lives in the committed review, not in chat. An ask for a yes states, in the message itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs ("What are the consequences of the yeses? What does that work even want to do? ... this is just pressuring me to give approval without understanding"); one ask per message; no label stands in for an explanation, and a new name is defined in the sentence that uses it; the recommendation comes after the explanation, in one line, never instead of it.
125	- **Ownership.** "I need to maintain some ownership of this work, even if we are doing agentic coding … I did not know what you did. I need to know what you did. And I need to be aware of those choices and decisions because I am the one carrying the responsibility for the consequences as a director of this revival": every re-approval row is gone through in detail, grouped by theme, and the count of reversals is not the measure. A decision made inside a worker's report and recorded in one line is a decision not made; flag it to him at the time.
126	- **The coordinator's standing goal** is to model what Pavol already knows and where his context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the minimal set of relevant facts at the level he needs to decide; machine tokens are spent on thinking so that human context is protected. This came out of a compaction that left him "out of control, unaware of crucial details" while the coordinator was "taking unauthorized initiative which compounded my sense of helplessness to steer the Fortress revival efforts". The coordinator's two hats: "executive assistant here in this Fortress Revival project, helping me, the director, find a way forward, and the analyst that finds out what the fuck happened, why, and how do we move forward".
127	- **While a batch runs**, no progress reports on it until it lands. He is on Central European time; check-in times are given to him in UTC and in his local time. The harness's stop-hook reminders about uncommitted or unpushed work are processed silently, declined without a word while work is in flight, and never mentioned to him. He reads on an iOS client that sometimes shows stale state; "is anything in flight" is answered from the tree, not from the UI.
128	- **Format.** "table formatted in this way is hard to read on mobile … we just need a list": no tables in chat, lists. "write the numbers just as K or M. I'm fine as a programmer understanding what a kilo is": never spelled-out thousands and millions, and a numbers message carries few numbers, each with its meaning. Time is spoken from the clock or the record (when a batch will probably land, when a check-in fires), never from feel, "yesterday", "this morning", "last night", when the events were minutes or hours apart (protocol § 3).

<!-- Handover note written by the coordinating session on 2026-09-14 and rewritten the same day after Runs C2 and C3 were integrated, so that the state of the C series and the APL side quest survives context compaction. Read this before touching either. Facts cite their files. The first section, added 2026-09-18, is where the work stands overall; the C series and the APL quest below it are parked. -->

# The C series and the APL side quest: state and what comes next

## Where the work stands

The goal is to finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it, not to redesign the language, with one program as the measuring stick: microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast (the root `CLAUDE.md` § Project goal; `coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-16).

The live thread is the one library. The interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`) is to become the library the compiler checks, and the work is to bring the compiled checker to accept it (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-21). Between that library and bytecode stands the checker, not desugaring or code generation; it reports 1 error on the library since climb batch 9, unchanged by climb batch 10 (the `isLeftZero` pair of `LexicographicReduction`, row 582, his choice, one error at two locations; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-10/gate/checker-count.txt`), 56 from climb batch 8, 59 from climb batch 7b (`FortressLibrary` 132 to 106 and `RangeInternals` 18 to 12 by rung L, the one library's refused overload families repaired by its own exclusions and `openRange`'s typecase: `MIN` 4, `MAX` 4, `openRangeHelper` 3, three juxtaposition and two `seq` errors gone, rung C's two `cond` errors cleared by L's api line), 75 from climb batch 7C (`FortressLibrary` 2 to 132 by rung Y, each error counted twice: `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause now checks as written, so the api's hierarchy pass no longer stops it and its 66 overloading and return-type errors are counted for the first time, row 459 closed; `RangeInternals` 18 unchanged), 10 from climb batch 7R (`RangeInternals` 42 to 18 by rung J, the one library's scalar ranges over `ZZ32` alone; `FortressLibrary` 2 unchanged), 22 from climb batch 7 (`FortressLibrary` 38 to 2, rung H having cleared the 18 instantiation-exclusion errors and the api still stopping at its hierarchy pass on `AnyIntegral`'s `comprises` clause, counted twice, item 21 of `coordinator/PLAN.md`; 5	
6	# Working in the Fortress revival repository
7	
8	This repository revives Sun's Fortress language. Two execution paths share one parser and the early phases: walk, the interpreter (`bin/fortress P.fss`), and the bytecode compiler (`bin/fortress compile P.fss`, then `bin/fortress run P`). Each has its own library today. The goal is one library, the interpreter's, that the compiled type checker accepts and the compiler compiles (the switch-over), and then the model program, microGPT, compiled and fast. The original tree, the historical artifact being revived, is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.
9	
10	## Rules that hold everywhere
11	
12	- Every edit under the original tree is test first: the test written, seen failing through the harness, then the fix, then the test seen passing. The test stays in the corpus.
13	- The suite's verdict is the check. A value that matters is asserted inside a test. Nobody compares the corpus's printed outputs or adds expected-output files.
14	- Nothing is built or run twice on the same code. A measurement the record holds is cited, never repeated. A log that finished stands unless the tree changed after it.
15	- Never wipe the Fortress caches: recompile what you edited.
16	- The library's own way first. The specification is the standard, and every change to it takes the revision form.
17	- Every claim is checked against a primary source: the code, the specification, a run. Reproduce before explaining, and change one variable per step. Where git does not record who wrote something, the attribution is reconstructed, never guessed, and no credit is claimed for the revival anywhere committed.
18	- Long commands (a build, a suite, the distance stage) run in the background and are polled, as the `remote-container` skill says. Never pipe `ant` through `tail`.
19	- Commit only the paths you wrote: never scratch, never a model identifier. The curator decides what is committed.
20	- Every report names each defect's home, each decision with its alternatives and evidence, and each reserved stop the work met, and asks the curator nothing (`references/area-records.md`, "What every report holds").
21

5	
6	# The container and the session
7	
8	The session is one process in a cloud container. The platform stops that process about every 13 hours and when the session goes idle, can restart the VM under it, and can lose the container outright. A stop or a restart keeps the disk; a lost container keeps only what was pushed. Running agents survive neither: after a stop they are resumed or relaunched.
9	
10	## Rules that hold everywhere
11	
12	- A command that may run longer than a minute or two runs in the background with a log, and is polled in steps under 270 s. Stop only your own processes.
13	- No single wait outlasts the prompt cache: under five minutes for a subagent, under an hour for the main session.
14	- Never stop a turn while agents run in the background: it kills them. A message kills nothing.
15	- After any stop, restart or loss, read what is on disk and what is pushed before starting anything again. A Workflow run is resumed, not relaunched.
16	- Nothing that takes hours lives only on disk: push as you go (how, for this repository: the `fortress-repo` skill, committing).
17	- A step the automatic permission check refuses is not pursued by another route or in a later turn.

5	
6	# The coordinator and the curator
7	
8	The coordinating session is the revival's main session. It keeps the project's memory, delegates the work to agents, judges what they return, and brings to the curator what only the curator can decide. The curator is the person who curates this restoration: the curator decides what is committed and what the agents are asked to do, and carries the responsibility for the consequences. The curator's attention is the scarcest thing the project spends; machine tokens go to thinking so that it is kept.
9	
10	## Rules that hold everywhere
11	
12	- A decision taken inside a worker's report or a batch is not made until the curator has seen it: it is listed for review or put to the curator, never left as a line in a report.
13	- One ask per message, in the ask form, in plain text in chat, never in a dialog tool.
14	- A closed decision is not reopened or re-asked, and a step a yes already covers is taken without asking again. Search POSITIONS before putting anything to the curator.
15	- Time is read from the clock or the record, never guessed.
16	- Delegate by default. The coordinator's context is spent on judgement, not on reading.
17	- When a goal is unclear, ask; when you act on one reading of it, say which.
18	- These rules serve purposes, and the purposes govern. When following a wording would defeat its purpose or make things worse, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. A rule is weighed by what it costs against what it protects.
19	- Effort and record stay in proportion: a side remark changes behaviour, not the record. When something is going wrong (a file growing, a rule making clutter, reports nobody asked for), propose the fix before the curator has to point it out.
20	
21	## Failures to watch for
22	
23	- Walls of text and the clever register; time guessed instead of read.
24	- A fork put to the curator before the library's own way was checked.
25	- A standing order or a technique invented when the record held one, or lost to a compaction and asked again.
26	- A correction appended instead of the line fixed; one remark of the curator's written into several files.
27	- A rule followed to the letter where that made clutter, or applied where its purpose did not hold.
28	- A brief that told a worker to distrust the record, so that it measured again what was on file.
29	- Scratch committed as evidence, and long runs awaited by agents with large contexts, so that the work paid more to record and to wait than to change Fortress.

1	# Build, caches, and what to rebuild after an edit
2	
3	## Every shell
4	
5	    cd <tree>                                   # the main tree or your own worktree
6	    source explorations/experiment/env.sh
7	
8	`env.sh` sets `JAVA_HOME` (JDK 25), `FORTRESS_HOME` (the tree the script sits in), `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m"`, unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` (the proxy's trust-store flags break ant's JVM forks), and deletes `/tmp/fortress*rats`. Source it once per shell, never in the middle of a run: another agent's live parser directories may be in `/tmp`. Every run that imports a grammar leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! parser directory, `fortress<random>rats`, in the JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it; hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance and broke tool output. Check `df -h /` before a long run (reading it, and the allowance: the `remote-container` skill). Check that `echo $FORTRESS_HOME` prints the tree you mean, because `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. When other agents share the machine, also keep your temporary files in your own tree:
9	
10	    export TMPDIR=<tree>/tmp
11	    export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=<tree>/tmp"
12	
13	## Building
14	
15	`ant compileAll`, from the tree's root, is the only build (`ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub).
16	
17	- About 25 to 60 s on a built tree, about 80 s from nothing.
18	- It deletes `default_repository/caches` whole before compiling, `global.map` with it. Like the rest of the caches that file is untracked and ignored, and the linker writes it afresh on the next run, so nothing is restored and `git status` shows nothing from the build.
19	- Before the next compiled run, the library order (below) must run again. Walk, `harness-one.sh`, the checker measurements and the two ant suites need nothing more.
20	- If it fails: fix the error and run it again. The caches are already gone, so there is nothing else to clear. Then run the library order.
21	- Neither test target compiles: a suite run on a stale `ProjectFortress/build` silently tests the previous code.
22	
23	Toolchain traps and generated sources: `toolchain.md`.
24	
25	## The caches
26	
27	`default_repository/caches/` (gitignored, all of it):
28	
29	- `analyzed_cache/`, `*parsed_cache/`: front-end analysis, each entry named by a hash of its source's absolute path, with that path inside it.
30	- `interpreter_cache/`, `environment_cache/`: walk.
31	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar per compiled component; library jars have api-qualified names (`fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`).
32	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: wrappers for `import java` natives.
33	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice; when it is missing the linker writes an empty one (`linker/RepoState.java:366-385`), in a private caches folder too.
34	
35	An entry is used when it is not older than its source, and a changed api makes everything that imports it stale. Because entries are keyed by absolute path, a plain copy of another tree's caches does not work; seed instead (`worktrees.md`).
36	
37	Only `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`) and a direct walk run read `default_repository/caches`. `harness-one.sh`, the checker count, the distance stage, the ladder driver and both ant suites use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), so they need neither the library order nor a warm cache. A private cache directory outside `tmp/` is not gitignored.
38	
39	## After an edit, what to rebuild
40	
41	Never wipe the caches: recompile what you edited. The advice to wipe in `explorations/repo-internals.md` does not hold.
42	
43	- The `.fss` of a compiler-library component (`LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin`, `Library/CompilerLibrary`, `Library/CompilerAlgebra`, `Library/CompilerSystem`), and not its `.fsi`: `fortress compile` that component alone (CompilerBuiltin about 60 s, CompilerLibrary about 25 s, the others 2 to 16 s). Programs need no recompile.
44	- The `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra, the roots every api depends on: all five in the library order, about 100 s. `CompilerSystem.fsi`: CompilerSystem alone.
45	- A file of the interpreter's library (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and the rest): nothing. Walk re-reads it on its next run, compiled programs do not link it yet, and the checker measurements read it from source.
46	- Java or Scala: `ant compileAll`, then the library order before the next compiled run.
47	- A changed signature of a native helper (`nativeHelpers/`): also delete its stale class under `default_repository/caches/nativewrapper_cache/`, or the run links the old signature.
48	
49	Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it. Skip the step above and a body edit runs the old code with no warning; an api edit dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
50	
51	The library order, about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll` (AnyType 17, CompilerBuiltin 63, CompilerLibrary 27, CompilerAlgebra 2, CompilerSystem 2):
52	
53	    cd ProjectFortress
54	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
55	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
56	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
57	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
58	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
59	
60	Symptoms:
61	
62	- `NoSuchMethodError` (for example on `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println` or `coerce_ZZ32`), or `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`: a component was not recompiled after an edit or after `ant compileAll`, and the run fell back to the frozen bootstrap stubs in `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`. Recompile the component, or run the library order. "Unable to read serialized data ... relink" is likewise a stale cache, not a compiler bug: recompile in the library order.
63	- A `fortress compile` whose source has not changed writes nothing and exits 0.
64	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs keep linking the old jar, silently, until you fix the error and compile that component again.
65	- A library order that exits 0 can still leave the bytecode cache empty; running the same commands one at a time produced the jars.
66	
67	Keeping the caches through a Java rebuild, `ant -Dcache0=/nonexistent -Dcache1=/nonexistent compileAll`, is safe only for an edit that cannot change a cached form: walk's evaluator and natives (`interpreter/evaluator/`, `interpreter/glue/`), the bodies of run-time classes with no signature change, the test harness, `Shell`'s options. Anything the library's compile runs (the parser, the AST, the disambiguator, the checkers, the desugarers, the code generator, `NamingCzar`, `OverloadSet`, `interpreter/rewrite/`) needs the plain `ant compileAll`. Nothing checks a kept entry against the compiler, so a stale one stays until the caches are deleted. Plain `ant compileAll` is the default.
68	
69	## Name resolution
70	
71	`fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` found wins, so a file in the directory you run from shadows the library. A component's file name without `.fss` must equal its component name. An api name both libraries use breaks one of them, which is why the compiler's apis are `Compiler`-prefixed. The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`; `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars. When paths misbehave, `repository/ProjectProperties.java` is what resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
72	
73	Deeper: `explorations/repo-internals.md` (architecture, cache anatomy); what each change reaches: `explorations/coordinator/map/README.md`, section 7.

2	
3	Read this when the build itself fails or behaves oddly, when changing JDKs or the build file, or before editing anything generated.
4	
5	- scalac runs through `scala.tools.nsc.Main`, since Scala 2.13 has no ant tasks. ASM is vendored in `ProjectFortress/third_party/asm/`, and Fortress's own `asmbytecodeoptimizer.Opcodes` shadows `org.objectweb.asm.Opcodes` in that package. Sources compile as UTF-8.

Edit the input, never the output. Churn in generated sources after a build is a regression to investigate, never noise to revert. scalac arity errors in `S*Pattern` nodes mean the generated nodes are stale: `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast && ant compileAll`.

1	# Worktrees, one build shared, and the old code beside the new
2	
3	Read this when several agents work at once, or when you need the behaviour of the code before your edit.
4	
5	## One build, many worktrees
6	
7	Build one tree at the base commit once, and seed every other worktree from it instead of building each one.
8	
9	The base build is a clean worktree at the base commit, built in place by ant, about 200 s:
10	
11	    git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach /home/user/fortress-base <base-commit>
12	    cd /home/user/fortress-base && source explorations/experiment/env.sh
13	    ant compileAll
14	    # the library order (build-and-caches.md), then warm walk's caches:
15	    bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
16	
17	From then on nobody compiles, builds or runs anything in it except through `old-fortress.sh` (below). The seeding script refuses a base that is no longer clean.
18	
19	Seeding a worktree takes about 3 s and 206 MB. The result runs walk and the compiled path at once, with the library already compiled:
20	
21	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
22	
23	- `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>` (default: the base's commit). `-` makes a detached worktree instead.
24	- Exit 2 means the base is not built or not clean, and nothing was made. Make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so.
25	- A worktree that already has a build is left alone, so a relaunch keeps its own build; `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
26	- It lists the library sources that differ from the base. Recompile them (`build-and-caches.md`) before a compiled run.
27	- It warns when `ProjectFortress/src` differs from the base: the copied build is the base's. Run `ant compileAll` (it recompiles exactly the differing files), then run the library order.
28	- The base's file dates must be a build's: a base built in place by ant, or one seeded by this script.
29	
30	Never symlink or plainly copy another tree's build or caches: cache entries are keyed by absolute path, and a symlinked build makes every cache path resolve to the other tree. The script translates the paths.
31	
32	Each agent works only in its own worktree, and two agents never compile into one cache: every compile rewrites cache files of the tree it runs in. Scratch goes under `<worktree>/tmp/` (gitignored). Set up each shell as `build-and-caches.md` says, and check that `echo $FORTRESS_HOME` prints your worktree.
33	
34	## The old code beside the new
35	
36	To see how the base's code behaves once your worktree holds an edit (a test seen failing, a program compared old against new), never revert and rebuild your worktree. Run the base build through `old-fortress.sh`, with a private caches folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
37	
38	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
39	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # compiled path ...
40	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then run
41	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
42	
43	The interpreter harness on the base's code:
44	
45	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
46	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
47	
48	- The tool sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private folder, overriding what `env.sh` set. On first use it fills the folder with a copy of the base's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s); later runs reuse it.
49	- Every cache file a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing it writes under the base stays (the parser's empty error logs beside a library source are removed at once). Several such runs at once, from several agents, are safe.
50	- Keep the folder and your programs outside the base build: the tool refuses a folder inside it (exit 2), and a program's own logs go beside the program.
51	- Never run the base build's `bin/fortress` without the tool: that compiles into the base's own caches.
52	- Any copy of the tool works, since it runs the base build named by its first argument.
53	
54	A harness run against another build's classes must set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to that build's caches as well as passing `-Dfortress.caches`: the `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process, whose class path comes from `FORTRESS_CACHES`.

1	# Running tests
2	
3	## The two suites
4	
5	- `ant testFast`: four tracks in parallel, each a forked JVM with its own caches. compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`. othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`, the longest track, which sets the wall clock. misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes. About 9 to 11 minutes, about 1,800 tests.
6	- `ant testSystem`: `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's corpus, in four shards. About 3 to 4 minutes, about 500 tests.
7	- The exact counts and times of the last landed run are in the newest gate summary:
8	
9	      git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
10	
11	- Run them after `ant compileAll` on the code you mean: neither compiles. Never run both at once, since both delete and reuse `ProjectFortress/test-caches`. Results land in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/<track>/TEST-<class>.txt`.
12	- `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures. "Tests expected to pass are failing!" is the same verdict, so do not grep for it separately.
13	- Both pin `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` inside `build.xml`, whatever the calling shell exports, and give each JVM 768 MB.
14	- The shards split one sorted list by index, so a file added to `tests/` moves every later test to another shard: compare only the sum of the four. A suite whose count fell almost always means a `.test` file or a `tests=` line went missing.
15	- Start them in the background and poll (the `remote-container` skill, long commands). Never pipe `ant` through `tail`: the verdict is at the end.
16	
17	## One test, or a few
18	
19	Interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`), from the tree's root with `env.sh` sourced:
20	
21	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
22	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
23	
24	It runs `SystemJUTest`, the class the shards run, with testSystem's JVM settings and an empty private cache, over a directory holding only the files you name. Name a test's `X.test` (its keys for a refusal at load) beside its `X.fss`. 15 to 25 s, most of it analysing the library. Several files go in one call, one JVM.
25	
26	For the real diagnostic the harness hides:
27	
28	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress tests/X.fss
29	
30	`bin/fortress` gives its JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set (`env.sh` sets 4 GB; the harness uses 768 MB), and a test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third.
31	
32	Compiled tests (`.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/`, `other_compiler_tests/`), after the library order (`build-and-caches.md`):
33	
34	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
35	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test
36	
37	It runs `fortress junit` once over the list, compile and link tests before run tests, and removes the named components' cache entries before and after. It sources the `env.sh` of the tree it sits in, so run your own tree's copy. Without `ONE_JVM=1` each file gets its own JVM. By hand, one file:
38	
39	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test
40	
41	Run all the new files of one corpus together, in one JVM, as the suite does: a test that passes alone can fail beside others.
42	
43	One unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`, about 90 s, most of it ant scanning `build/`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
44	
45	One track of testFast, whole (`CompilerJUTest`, `LibraryJUTest` or `OtherCompilerJUTest`), in its own JVM with a private cache, as `harness-one.sh` runs `SystemJUTest` and the `fastTrack` macro of `build.xml` runs the tracks; about 7 minutes for the compiler track:
46	
47	    S=<tree>/tmp/track-compiler ; rm -rf $S ; mkdir -p $S/caches $S/tmp ; printf '\0\0\0\0' > $S/caches/global.map
48	    CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
49	    cd ProjectFortress && FORTRESS_THREADS=1 FORTRESS_CACHES=$S/caches \
50	      java -Xmx768m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$S/tmp -Dfortress.caches=$S/caches -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 \
51	           -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.tests.unit_tests.CompilerJUTest > $S/out.txt 2>&1
52	
53	The verdict is the last lines: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. `ant testCompiler`, `ant testLibrary` and `ant testOtherCompiler` exist too, but each first runs `ant compileAll`, which deletes the tree's caches.
54	
55	Switches the harness reads: `-Dtests=<dir>` (SystemJUTest's directory), `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`, `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`, `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>` (each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`), and `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` or `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` to see the output of passing tests.
56	
57	## When a whole suite runs
58	
59	- The gate (`gate.md`) runs everything once, on a clean build of the tree that lands on `main`.
60	- An edit to the checker's or walk's Java or Scala may run the suite it reaches, whole, once per code state, after its last edit: the compiler and library tracks for the checker, `testSystem` for walk. Quote the verdict lines, the command and the commit. Nobody runs it again on that commit.
61	- Every other change runs only its own tests, through the scripts above, and leaves the rest to the gate. A change of tests, prose or records alone runs no whole suite.
62	- A tree already gated is gated again only when code it reads changed (`gate.md`).

1	# The gate
2	
3	The gate decides whether a tree lands on `main`. It runs once, on a clean build of that tree. A tree already gated is gated again only when it changed under `ProjectFortress/` (other than test files), `Library/` or `build.xml`:
4	
5	    git diff --quiet <gated-commit> HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library build.xml || echo "changed: gate again unless only test files moved"
6	
7	A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory. Changed test files alone are run through `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` instead (`tests-running.md`), the files of one corpus together in one JVM, and the gate's tables stand.
8	
9	## What it runs
10	
11	On a clean build, in order: `df -h /` (under 1 GB free, sweep `/tmp/fortress*rats`, `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` and `ProjectFortress/test-caches`); `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`; `ant compileAll`; the distance stage started in the background; the library order; `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, with zero failures; each suite's count compared with the newest landed summary (`tests-running.md`), red when one fell or a suite is gone; the four-thread atomic runs; the ladder regression; the checker count. The checker count is red only on a new crash line, a stale shadow or a missing total; the distance is reported and never red (`checker-measurements.md`).
12	
13	It takes about 25 minutes: `ant compileAll` 25 to 60 s, the library order about 110 s, testFast 9 to 11 min, testSystem 3 to 4 min, the atomic runs about 1 min, the ladder about 4 min, the checker count 20 s to 2.5 min. The distance stage (13 to 24 min on one core) runs beside the rest from just after `ant compileAll`.
14	
15	The atomic runs. The suites run at one thread and cannot see a lost update or a race in the class loader's first load, so fourteen compiled programs run three times each at four threads, 42 lines, from `ProjectFortress/` after the library order:
16	
17	    for p in AtomicTopLevelObjectVar AtomicTopLevelVar MutableTopLevelVarInLoop FirstLoadThreadsRungG \
18	             atomic0 atomic1 atomic2 atomic3 atomic4 atomic5 atomic6 \
19	             nestedTransactions0 nestedTransactions1 nestedTransactions2 ; do
20	      d=other_compiler_tests ; [ -f compiler_tests/$p.fss ] && d=compiler_tests
21	      timeout -k 5 300 ../bin/fortress compile $d/$p.fss >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "$p COMPILE-FAILED" ; continue ; }
22	      for i in 1 2 3 ; do
23	        out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$?
24	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && { out=$(FORTRESS_THREADS=4 timeout -k 5 120 ../bin/fortress run $p 2>&1) ; rc=$? ; }
25	        case "$out" in *FAIL*) r=FAIL ;; *PASS*) r=PASS ;; *) r="NO-PASS rc=$rc" ;; esac
26	        [ $rc -eq 124 ] && r=TIMEOUT-TWICE
27	        echo "$p run$i threads=4 $r"
28	      done
29	    done
30	
31	Red: any FAIL, NO-PASS, COMPILE-FAILED or TIMEOUT-TWICE. A single timeout that passes on its re-run is not red.
32	
33	The ladder regression compiles and runs the files listed in `explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt`, compared with the baseline's recorded phase and output (`raw/`), and compiles only (never runs) the eighteen microGPT components, held at their recorded phase (`microgpt-phase.md`). Copy the subset driver `explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and the baseline's `classify.py`, `report.py`, `microgpt-phase.sh` and `microgpt-phase.py` into a directory under your `tmp/`, and point `OUT` and `LADDER_ROOT` in the two shell drivers there. Put copies of `default_repository/caches`, taken right after the library order, at `$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches` and `$LADDER_ROOT/pristine`, or the driver rebuilds the library (about 145 s). The file list:
34	
35	    tail -n +2 explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/pass-list.txt | cut -f1 | sed 's|/|\t|' > <dir>/subset.txt
36	
37	Run `run-subset.sh`, then `classify.py` in that directory for `ladder.tsv`, then `microgpt-phase.sh` and `microgpt-phase.py` for the eighteen: about 200 s for the files and 35 s for the eighteen. Compare with the baseline file by file: a phase lower than recorded (in the order parse, disambiguate, typecheck, codegen, link, run, pass) is DOWN, a file with no output is MISSING, and output that differs once `Operation took <n>ms` is masked is STDOUT; each is red unless the change named it in advance as expected. A higher phase is UP, which is progress. Never run the whole-corpus driver with its default root: that root is shared, and its cache pruning corrupts a parallel run. A change's own ladder subset is the files whose recorded first error in `baseline-2026-09-19/raw/` names something it touched; their before is the last landed ladder table, or the baseline's output.
38	
39	The microGPT programs themselves never run in the gate.

1	# Writing a test
2	
3	## Test first, and the test stays
4	
5	Every edit under the original tree (everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`) starts from a failing test added to the corpus:
6	
7	1. Write the test: the essence of the defect as a clean minimal program, not the shape a probe happened to meet it in.

1	# The gap ledger and the coordinator's records
2	
3	The record is the project's memory. Read the slice you need and cite what it holds instead of measuring it again. Apart from the coordinator's boot, nobody reads its big files whole.
4	
5	## Finding things
6	
7	Print slices of the record, whole entries in bounded parts:
8	
9	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
10	    $T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'            # the FACTS.md entry whose bold title holds them
11	    $T 'section:HEADING'             # every FACTS.md entry of a section
12	    $T 'ledger:424'                  # one row of the gap ledger
13	    $T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'  # one of the curator's decisions
14	    $T 'index:WORDS'                 # the INDEX.md lines on a topic, one per note
15	    $T 'map:README.md#Touch this'    # a section of a territory map
16	    $T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'            # a section of any note, or of a .tex chapter
17	    $T --check ...                   # where each key matches and its size; --part N continues; --help
18	
19	The files:
20	
21	- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established, each fact with its source and its test, cited by its bold title, or by its opening words where it has none.
22	- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: what the curator has decided and already knows. A closed decision is not reopened.
23	- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line per standalone note. Search it before saying anything is absent.
24	- `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`: the phases and the open issues, in the order they need deciding.
25	- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`: the known gaps, one row each.
26	- `explorations/coordinator/map/`: `README.md` (section 7: what each change reaches, which tests guard it, where the gate is blind), `spec-to-implementation.md` (where a fix belongs), `modules-and-phases.md`, `test-coverage.md`, `design-intent-sources.md` (where the designers' intent is written), `dormant-code.md` (code present and switched off).
27	- `explorations/repo-internals.md`: architecture, name resolution, cache anatomy, git archaeology. A `git log` of a directory is useless here (the history has parentless roots); use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
28	- `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`, its first section: where the work stands.
29	
30	The 2012 tree's own READMEs describe their era, not the current tree: check a claim of theirs against the code before acting on it.
31	
32	## The repository's history
33	
34	The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository: 5,397 trunk commits from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31, ending at `a874948ac`, with twelve old branches and the `1.0` tag. Everything after `a874948ac` is the revival's own work. The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a history walk from `HEAD` stops early; how to find who wrote something, and where the lineage after 2012 comes from, is `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
35	
36	## Practices
37	
38	- A measurement the record holds is cited with its source and never repeated. Measure again only when the tree has changed under it, and say what changed. Measure only what is new.
39	- Before doing something a new way, search the record for how it was done last time.
40	- A timing names its machine: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair taken in one run measures a difference. No timing of the interpreter is taken.
41	- A report cites the tree at file:line and quotes results, two to five lines, each with its command. It never cites a file under `tmp/`.
42	
43	## The gap ledger
44	
45	- One row per claim, with a status (`POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`), a class (`implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`) and how to reproduce it, under sections by area.
46	- Rows are never renumbered or moved: reports everywhere cite them by number. A new issue gets a new row with a new number; a fixed one is closed in place.
47	- Rows are the bug reports the work fixes: a fix begins by committing the row's reproduction, as a clean minimal test, to the corpus (`tests-writing.md`).
48	
49	## FACTS, POSITIONS and the rest
50	
51	- FACTS and POSITIONS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. A wrong line is rewritten in place; the provenance lives in `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`. A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, under a bold title, pointing to the report that holds the detail.
52	- One home per thing: the curator's words are written once, in POSITIONS, and everything else points there.
53	- The record is updated in the same commit as the work that establishes the fact or takes the decision.
54	- An agent working beside others does not edit `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, `PLAN.md`, `INDEX.md`, the ledger, the handover, `CLAUDE.md`, `explorations/protocol.md`, the tools under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `.claude/`: parallel edits of those files conflict. It writes the lines for them in its report (the FACTS entry, the ledger note, the plan line) as finished prose, for whoever folds them in.
55	- Everything of ours lives under `explorations/`. `research/decks/` holds copyrighted material, is gitignored and is never committed.
56	
57	## What every report holds
58	
59	Every agent that finds or decides something, in an exploration or a batch, puts it in its report in this form, whatever else its brief asks for:
60	
61	- **Defects.** Each defect measured, with its home named: an assertion in a gated test, a gated `XXX` test, a test pinning today's behaviour with a ledger row, or the row alone (`tests-writing.md`, "Where a measured defect goes"). A row is in the ledger's form above, written in the report as finished prose when you may not edit the ledger.
62	- **Decisions.** Each choice made among alternatives, named as a decision apart from the findings: what was chosen, the alternatives considered, and the evidence, cited. Where the record holds no position, none is invented: say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
63	- **Stops met.** Each stop the brief reserves that the work met, listed as met, with its evidence, including one met on part of the work.
64	- **Nothing more.** The report does not choose which of its items anyone reviews, and the agent asks the curator nothing: an open question goes in the report, as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
65

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	The curator decides what is committed. Commit only when your task says to.
4	
5	## What may be committed
6	
7	- Committed: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script that is reusable.
8	- Never: captured outputs, logs, raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists, or any other scratch. Scratch lives under your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored; a private cache directory outside `tmp/` is not.
9	- Never: a model identifier (a model is named by its tier: Fable, Opus, Sonnet); a copyrighted PDF or deck (`research/decks/` is gitignored; cite such a source by its Wayback URL; `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries with brief attributed quotations); `HANDOVER.md` or ZIP contents without the curator's go. The curator's email is for attribution only.
10	- No self-credit anywhere committed. Provenance and rationale go in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
11	
12	## How
13	
14	- Commit only the paths you wrote, as you go, in one command, never a directory copy and never `git add -A`:
15	
16	      git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
17	
18	- Read a staged change of more than a few hundred lines with `git diff --cached --stat` before committing it.
19	- An edit under the original tree (anything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`): the test comes before the fix (`tests-writing.md`), and the commit message flags the edit as one of the original tree.
20	- The footer, exactly as below. It names no model, whatever another footer the harness suggests:
21	
22	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
23	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
24	
25	## Pushing
26	
27	- A worker on its own branch pushes that branch as it works (`git push -u origin <branch>` the first time), so that a lost container loses nothing. It never touches the main tree, `/home/user/fortress`.
28	- To `main`: only after `git log origin/main..main` shows nothing but your own commits, and then both, in this order:
29	
30	      git push origin main
31	      git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
32	
33	  The second keeps current the branch the container is re-provisioned from (the `remote-container` skill, a lost container). No other branch is pushed without permission (the transcript branches excepted).
34	- A commit on `main` is pushed right after it is made, so that nothing on `main` waits on disk.
